title: Rust vs Go for backend services in 2026

slides.name: Rust and Go in 2026

image.alt: Abstract metallic service modules connected by flowing paths against a dark navy background

blocks.text: Rust vs Go: ==two ways to build reliable backend services==
Memory model, developer signals, and a practical decision rule.

slides.notes: Frame this as a trade-off discussion, not a universal language ranking. We will compare memory and concurrency models, show a deliberately small code example, then separate developer-survey interest from actual backend adoption.

slides.name: The memory-model divide

blocks.text: Rust checks ownership at compile time; Go ==collects memory at runtime==

children.text: Memory safety without a garbage collector.
Ownership and types catch many concurrency errors before execution.
Go 1.26 made its Green Tea collector the default.

sources.title: Understanding Ownership - The Rust Programming Language
Fearless Concurrency - The Rust Programming Language

slides.notes: Ownership is a compile-time discipline: values have owners, and borrowing permits access without transferring ownership. The Rust book also describes how ownership and types make many concurrency mistakes compile-time errors. Go uses garbage collection, so the trade-off is a different memory-management model rather than simply one language being faster.

slides.name: What changed for Go in 2026

blocks.text: Go’s 2026 updates improve its runtime; ==the models stay different==

rows: Many errors caught by ownership and types
Ownership model remains the comparison point
1.26: Green Tea GC default; 1.27: generic methods
blocks.caption: Go 1.26 projects 10–40% less GC overhead in GC-heavy programs—not 10–40% more service throughput.

sources.title: Understanding Ownership - The Rust Programming Language
Fearless Concurrency - The Rust Programming Language

slides.notes: Go 1.26 enabled Green Tea GC by default; its projected 10–40% reduction concerns GC overhead for workloads that heavily use the collector. That number is not a service-throughput benchmark and says nothing quantitative about Rust versus Go. Go 1.27 adds generic methods and reiterates Go 1 compatibility; assess these updates separately from the architectural choice.

slides.notes: The left chart has language users as its denominator; the right chart uses survey respondents. They cannot be interpreted as the same measure, and neither is production backend market share. In the 2025 survey Rust scores 72.4% versus Go 56.5% on admired, and 29.2% versus 23.4% on desired.

blocks.text: Choose by the service constraint, ==then test the real workload==

children.text: No GC and compile-time ownership are core requirements.
Managed memory and Go 1 compatibility fit the team.

blocks.text: Next step: prototype one representative endpoint; measure latency, memory and iteration time.

sources.title: Understanding Ownership - The Rust Programming Language
Fearless Concurrency - The Rust Programming Language

slides.notes: Close with a decision procedure rather than a winner. If avoiding GC and enforcing ownership during compilation are explicit service requirements, evaluate Rust. If managed memory and Go's compatibility commitment fit team needs, evaluate Go. In either case, prototype a representative endpoint and measure the metrics that matter to this service.
